strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: safe scaling of LLM-based multi-agent systems, with compelling motivation in Figure 1
Sound theoretical framework: contextual bandit formalization with formal monotonic improvement guarantee (Theorem 4.3) and elegant conservative embedding mechanism
Thoughtful system design combining agent-conditioned task synthesis, auditable natural-language memory, and conservative fallback—more interpretable than end-to-end learned approaches

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple router models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemini), benchmarks (GAIA, HLE), and settings (clean/malfunctioning pools) with detailed case studies demonstrating failure modes and solutions
Strong reproducibility: extensive appendices provide agent configurations, prompts, memory schemas, complete proofs, and detailed case studies enabling reproduction
Effective demonstration that adaptive router updates—not just stronger backbone models—are crucial for robust scaling (Qwen-3 with 10 agents outperforms fixed-pool GPT-5 with 3 agents)
weaknesses: Severe experimental scale limitation: validated only up to 10 agents despite claiming applicability to 'Agentic Web' with millions; no cost-benefit analysis or scaling trajectory provided; unclear if approach remains effective at realistic scales

Significant theory-practice gap: assumes stationary distribution and verifiable rewards but uses synthesized tasks not from true distribution; Assumption B.1 (non-interfering expansion) is strong and unvalidated; warm-up task distribution match to deployment distribution not empirically verified

Underspecified memory update mechanism: semantic trust region not formally defined; procedure for generating candidate memories from evidence buffer B_k lacks algorithmic detail; reconciliation of conflicting evidence unclear; sensitivity to trust-region radius δ not ablated

Limited technical novelty: task synthesis directly follows Guo et al. (2024), memory-based routing is established work, trust-region updates adapt standard TRPO; contribution is primarily engineering combination of existing techniques without significant algorithmic innovation

Weak baseline comparisons: 'naive scale-up' is a strawman; missing comparisons to lightweight alternatives (in-context learning, simple fine-tuning, confidence-weighted heuristics); Table 1 shows Qwen-3 (10 agents, 55.15%) barely exceeds GPT-5 (3 agents, 54.55%), questioning complexity justification

Modest experimental improvements: GAIA shows +23% relative gain but from weak baseline; HLE result (19.90%) essentially matches GPT-5 (19.63%); no statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; results appear to be single runs

Missing critical ablations: no separate evaluation of task synthesis vs. memory updates; no sensitivity analysis for number of warm-up tasks or memory schema design; unclear component contributions to overall performance

Generalization concerns: all experiments use CAMEL framework on factual QA with verifiable answers; no evaluation on open-ended generation, reasoning tasks, or domains without clear correctness criteria; applicability beyond this setting unclear

Practical assumptions not validated: assumes accurate/complete agent cards (often unavailable in practice); requires verifiable rewards (not universal); memory frozen after each round without justification; synthesis quality cannot guarantee discovery of all failure modes

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence of performance collapse during naive scaling (Figure 1)
Comprehensive approach integrating formalization (contextual bandit), methodology (task synthesis + memory updates), theory (Theorem 4.3), and extensive experiments
Solid theoretical contribution: conditional monotonicity guarantee under explicit assumptions (C.1, C.2) with empirical validation
Excellent experimental design including ablations, cross-router transfer studies, robustness testing, and detailed case studies demonstrating failure modes
Practical innovations: auditable natural-language memory, conservative fallback, semantic consistency checking, and trust-region constraints
Strong empirical results showing weak router (Qwen-3-30B) with MonoScale can match much stronger fixed-pool baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro)
Honest treatment of limitations: conditional guarantees, memory saturation concerns, web-scale scalability challenges, and ethical risks thoroughly discussed
High reproducibility: detailed agent configurations, memory schemas, algorithms, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited experimental scale: main results at N≤10 agents with only a 20-agent probe; significant gap between claimed Agentic Web scope and demonstrated scale
Strong theoretical assumptions (non-interfering expansion C.1, feasible fallback C.2) validated only at small scale (100 HLE tasks); robustness under realistic API drift and behavioral shifts unclear

Memory scalability inadequately addressed: fixed token budget, LLM-based consistency checking, and no analysis of degradation beyond N=10; semantic consistency relies on LLM calls introducing compounding errors

Modest theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.3 follows relatively directly from TRPO principles; lacks convergence analysis, sample complexity bounds, or regret characterization; no guidance for setting KL trust radius δ
Asymmetric experimental baselines: strong models (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro) only evaluated at fixed N=3, not with MonoScale memory applied due to non-monotonic scaling

Natural-language memory reliability not established at scale: routing decisions depend on LLM-generated text; cross-router transfer shows gaps (62.4% vs 58.8%); no structured representation comparison
Performance non-monotonicity in practice contradicts theory: local dip at N=6 (Appendix D.7) reveals tool-budget exhaustion not captured by theory-practice gap deserves more analysis
Gap between theory (continuous constrained optimization Eq. 11) and practice (discrete one-shot selection Algorithm 1) not formally justified
Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis for KL radius δ, no comparison to EvoRoute despite claiming complementarity, limited baseline diversity
Warm-up cost analysis insufficient: ~$19.50 per agent is only 2× cheaper than full evaluation; ROI marginal for rapid scaling or cost-sensitive deployments

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1) showing performance collapse in naive agent pool scaling
Solid theoretical contribution with monotonic improvement guarantee (Theorem 4.3) under clearly stated assumptions, with clean conservative lift construction
Practical and interpretable framework using frozen LLM with editable natural-language memory, avoiding parameter-inefficient fine-tuning

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (GAIA, HLE) with strong baselines (GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2), demonstrating that adaptive updates matter more than backbone strength
Robust validation including malfunctioning agent pools, ablation studies isolating contributions, and cross-router memory transfer experiments
Strong empirical results: Qwen-3-30B-A3B with MonoScale (55.15% at 10 agents) outperforms fixed-pool GPT-5 (54.55%); HLE improves from 11.70% to 19.88%
Detailed case studies (Appendix F) revealing concrete failure modes (cold-start misjudgment, brittle workflows) and how MonoScale resolves them
Honest discussion of limitations including non-interfering expansion assumptions, scalability constraints, and theory-practice gaps
weaknesses: Severe scalability limitations: main experiments only scale to 10 agents; admitted Agentic Web vision (millions of agents) requires future retrieval-based routing; no strategy provided for managing natural-language memory token-budget saturation at scale

Strong and potentially fragile assumptions: non-interfering expansion (Assumption C.1) breaks under environment drift and resource competition; feasible conservative fallback (C.2) assumes reliable LLM constraint adherence; empirical validation limited to GAIA/HLE

Theory-practice gap: theory assumes continuous trust-region optimization (Eq. 16) but practice uses one-shot selection from finite candidates (Algorithm 1); no analysis of approximation error or empirical validation that finite candidates preserve monotonicity guarantees

Finite-sample monotonicity violated: Figure 3 shows accuracy dip at N=6 (47.3% to 46.1%), contradicting monotonic improvement claims; while attributed to tool-budget exhaustion, this undermines practical utility of theoretical guarantees

Limited technical novelty: task synthesis increments Guo et al. (2024) by conditioning on agent cards; memory updates apply existing TRPO; natural-language memory explored in prior work; main contribution is combination and problem framing rather than new methods

Incomplete experimental comparisons: no direct comparison with other continual/online routing methods (EvoRoute mentioned as complementary but not compared); naive baselines don't use other adaptation strategies; cross-router transfer shows non-trivial gaps (62.4% vs 58.8%), suggesting router-specific factors dominate

Limited benchmark diversity and statistical rigor: GAIA and HLE-MCQ are specialized; multi-seed evaluation only on 40-task GAIA subset with 2-3% std dev; main results report single runs; generalization to other task distributions unclear

Memory management underspecified: semantic consistency check criteria not detailed; no analysis of candidate rejection frequency; missing pruning/consolidation strategy for memory growth; semantic drift over many expansions not studied

Moderate agent pool heterogeneity: test agents are fairly standard (Web, Code, Math, etc.); unclear how method handles truly brittle or adversarially designed agents; malfunctioning agent tests cover specific failure modes but not worst-case scenarios
